question: How do I calculate a crane's net capacity?

body.text: Practice: net capacity equals gross chart capacity minus all deductions. Find the gross value for your exact configuration and radius. Follow the chart notes to add up every deduction, such as hook blocks, ball, rigging and jib. Subtract that total. The load must fit within what is left. The rule text used here doesn't give this formula or list deductions, but it does set this limit:
The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

question: What items do I deduct from gross capacity?

body.text:
Practice: your load chart notes control. Common deductions to check:
• Main hook block
• Auxiliary block or headache ball
• Slings, shackles and other rigging
• Spreader bars, lifting beams, grabs and other below-the-hook gear
• Stowed or erected jib or extension
• Auxiliary boom head or other attachments
• Extra wire rope, if the chart requires it
Use actual or chart-listed weights. The rule text used here has no deduction list. It does require this:
The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

question: What is the difference between gross capacity and net capacity?

body.text: Practice: gross capacity is the chart value before deductions. Net capacity is what remains for the load after you subtract the deductions the chart requires. Don't treat the gross number as the weight of material you can pick. Read the chart notes to see what its values include. The rule text used here doesn't define either term. It does say:
The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

question: Can you show a worked example of a net capacity calculation?

body.text:
Practice example with made-up numbers. Use your own chart and gear weights.
Gross at your configuration and radius: 20,000 lb.
Main block 600 + headache ball 200 + spreader bar 500 + slings and shackles 300 = 1,600 lb of deductions.
Net: 20,000 − 1,600 = 18,400 lb.
A 17,000 lb load fits, with 1,400 lb left. A 19,000 lb load is 600 lb over, even though it is under gross. The limit is:
The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

question: Should I subtract rigging from gross capacity or add it to the load weight?

body.text:
Practice: either method gives the same pass or fail answer if used correctly.
• Gross minus all deductions = net. Compare it with the load alone.
• Load plus all deductions = total. Compare it with gross.
Don't mix them and count an item twice, and don't leave one out. Percent of capacity can differ between the two methods, so state which basis you used. Either way:
The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

question: Do I have to deduct a stowed jib when lifting off the main boom?

body.text: Practice: check the chart notes. Many telescopic (hydro) crane charts require a deduction for a stowed jib or extension when you lift from the main boom. The value to use is the one in that crane's chart or notes. It may not match the jib's actual weight, because where the weight sits affects capacity. Don't borrow a figure from another crane. The operating limit is:
The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

question: What do I deduct for an erected jib?

body.text:
Practice: first identify where you're lifting from.
• From the jib: use the jib chart for that length, offset and configuration, then apply its notes.
• From the main boom with the jib erected: use the main boom notes. They may require an erected-jib deduction, or may restrict or prohibit that lift.
Also check blocks, ball, rigging and other listed items. Don't assume the stowed-jib value applies. You must stay within this limit:
The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

question: Do I deduct the weight of the wire rope?

The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

question: Is net capacity limited by parts of line?

body.text: Practice: it can be. Check both the boom or jib chart and the reeving or line pull information for your parts of line and rope. The lower limit controls. A high chart value doesn't help if the reeving can't carry it. Check the chart notes for how to count block and rigging weight on the line, so you apply deductions correctly to each limit. The crane must stay within this limit:
The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

question: How do I figure net capacity when the radius or setup changes during the lift?

body.text: Practice: check the whole planned path, including pick, swing and set. For each radius, work area and configuration, find the gross value and apply the deductions. The load must fit at every point. The lowest net capacity along the path limits a load of fixed weight. For radius or boom length between chart values, follow the chart notes. Don't interpolate unless they allow it. At all times:
The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

question: Can I make the lift if the load is under gross capacity but over net capacity?

body.text: Practice: no, not when the chart requires those deductions. A load over correctly figured net capacity means load plus deductions is over gross. Stop and replan, for example by changing radius or configuration, then recalculate. The rule has this limit:
The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

question: Does the LMI reading already include the hook block and rigging, so I shouldn't deduct them again?

body.text: Practice: don't assume. Displays can differ in what the load reading includes, such as blocks, ball, rigging or rope. Check the operator's manual, the device settings and the chart notes. The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

question: How do I check someone else's net capacity calculation?

body.text:
Practice checklist:
• Chart matches the crane and its actual configuration
• Radius and work area cover the whole lift
• Chart notes were applied
• Every required deduction is listed once, with a reliable weight
• Reeving limit was checked
• Load plus deductions fits within gross
Also ask how the operator verified the load. The rule requires at least one listed method:
The operator must verify that the load is within the rated capacity of the equipment by at least one of the following methods:
